en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Thirty Birth Stories, Chapter on Kiṁchanda.
3. The Jayaddisa Jātaka:
“Ah, after a long time, today at the hour of the seventh meal, food has indeed appeared for me!”
“Who are you? Or from where do you come? Tell me this;
declare your birth as you are known.
“I am the King of Pañcāla, who has entered the hunt.”
"Jayaddisa by name is the son of Yadu whom you seek;
I am wandering through the marshes and forests.
Eat this spotted deer and release me today."
“While you yourself are selling your own crop,
you say, ‘This pleasure-park of mine is my food.
Having eaten that hunger-inducing pleasure-park, [you will suffer].”
"I shall eat later; it is not the time for lamentation.
"There is no release for me by means of a ransom;
I have gone for the sake of returning after the question has been answered."
Having given that promise to the brahmin,
I shall return again, guarding my truthfulness.
"What kind of deed do you regret?"
"O King, death is close at hand;
tell me that so that we may grant permission for our departure."
“I have made a promise to the brahmin;
that pledge I bound myself to has not been released.
Having fulfilled that pledge to the brahmin, [I shall go forth].”
“Guarding the truth, I shall return.
“The hope for wealth you formed for the brahmin—
that promise you made is not yet released.”
Having given that promise to the brahmin,
return again, guarding your truth.
And he was released from the hands of the man-eater.
Having gone to his own palace, he who desired pleasure,
having given that promise to the brahmin,
addressed his son Alīnasatta.
“Be consecrated to the kingship this very day;
practice the Dhamma toward yourself and toward others as well;
let there be no unrighteous conduct in your kingdom.”
“I am going to inform the man-eater.
“What deed did I do, O Lord, that I have displeased you?
I wish to hear about it.”
"Whatever glory you might exult in today within this kingdom,
I would renounce even that kingdom without you,
dear one. Neither by deed nor by word, O father..."
"I remember that I have indeed offended you greatly;
yet, having made a pact with the man-eater,
I shall go back again, guarding my truth."
“I shall go; stay right here.
There is no escape for you from that while you still live.
Even if you do go, O King—”
“I too shall go; we two shall not remain.
“Truly, dear father, this is the nature of beings;
death would be even more painful for me than that.”
"When Kammāsapāda has roasted you and,
having seized you, shall eat you at the stake of the tree—
then I will exchange my life for yours."
"Do not go to the man-eater's knowledge;
I shall give you my own life in exchange for this.
Therefore, I praise death over life."
Then the resolute prince,
having paid homage at the feet of his mother and father,
[departed]; his mother fell down in grief upon the earth.
His father, stretching out his arms, wept.
Having recognized that he was departing, the father,
with palms joined, paid homage while turning his back.
“King Soma and King Varuṇa,
Pajāpati, Candra, and Sūrya— protected by these, I have escaped from the man-eater.”
“Permitted, my dear, return in safety.
“That which the mother of Daṇḍaki’s king did for Rāma when he had gone away—
well-guarded, she brought him back in safety.”
I shall bring you safety;
by this truth may the gods take heed!
Permitted, my son, return in safety.
“Whether in public or in private,
I have never harbored ill-will toward any being, however defiled.
By this truth, may the gods remember me!”
“Permitted, brother, go back in safety.
“Since you do not hold me in high regard, O Lord,
nor am I even disliked by you in your mind;”
"By this truth, may the gods protect you;
permitted, O Lord, return in safety.
"How is it that you, so tall, upright, and with such a beautiful face, have come from [where]?"
"You do not know me living in the forest;
knowing me to be a hunter, a man-eater,
who would venture here seeking safety?"
“I know you, hunter, as a man-slayer;
I do not not know you dwelling in the forest.
And I am the son of Jayaddisa.”
"Eat me today for the sake of your father's release.
"I know you are Jayaddisa’s son,
for such is the complexion of both your faces."
“Only what is most difficult has been done by you,
who desire to deliver your father from death.
“I do not consider anything here to be difficult,” he replied.
Whoever desires the release of their father,
or for the sake of their mother, shall go to the next world and be endowed with happiness and heaven.
“I have never concealed my own evil deeds, whether in public or in private;
I am one who has fully understood birth and death.”
Just as it is for me here, so it shall be in the next world.
O one of great power, eat me now;
perform your duties with this body.
"I shall fall from the very top of this tree;
covering me, you must give me the meat.
"And if this is what pleases you, O Prince,"
"You have sacrificed your own life for the sake of your father's release;
therefore, indeed, you who are in such a hurry,
gather wood and kindle a fire with water."
Then indeed the steadfast prince,
having gathered wood and kindled a great fire, announced it.
“Now this great fire is ablaze!
Eat me now, you impetuous one!
Why do you look at me again and again with your hair standing on end?”
"In whatever way you have commanded me, covering me, in that very way I shall act for you.
"Who would deserve to eat such a person?"
One who would refuse such a speaker of truth— who stands firm in the Dhamma,
speaks the truth, and is generous— his head would shatter into seven pieces.
“Indeed, thinking him to be a brahmin,
the hare sacrificed his own body;
for that very reason, he became the lunar deity Candima.”
“O Yakkha, praised by the world, you are today like a wish-fulfilling cow.
“Like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu,
or like the sun shining on the fifteenth day, [I shine].”
Thus released from you, O man-eater,
shine forth in Kapila, O one of great power,
gladdening both your father and your mother.
"And may all your circle of kinsmen rejoice.
Then the steadfast prince,
with palms joined, addressed Poriyāsapurisāda in turn:
Permitted, safe, happy, and healthy,
he returned, his mind settled in Kapila.
All the people of the towns and the countryside [welcomed him].
Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors,
and foot-soldiers approached with palms joined in reverence,
saying: "Homage to you, O performer of difficult deeds!"
The Third Jātaka: The Story of Jayaddisa.
